scenes.title: Pleasure Defined
scenes.summary: Pleasure is a movement of the soul, a sudden and perceptible settling into its natural state, and pain the opposite. So it is pleasant to return to nature, to follow habit, which is like nature, and to be free of force ("every necessary thing is grievous"); ease, play, rest and sleep are pleasant.

scenes.title: Appetite, Memory and Hope
scenes.summary: Appetite is longing for the pleasant, irrational when it comes from the body, rational when it comes from persuasion. Since imagination is a weak perception, the pleasant lies in perceiving the present, remembering the past or hoping for the future.

scenes.title: Pleasures Remembered and Hoped For
scenes.summary: Even past toils are sweet to remember when one is safe; anger is "sweeter than dripping honey" because it hopes for revenge; the thirsty in a fever remember drinking; lovers talk and write of the beloved, and the pain of absence is the beginning of love; mourning too has its pleasure, as in the verse "in all of them he stirred the longing for lament."

scenes.title: Revenge, Victory, Honor and Change
scenes.summary: Revenge and victory are pleasant, and so are games, hunting, litigation and disputation; honor and reputation, above all from those we respect; being loved, admired and flattered; doing the same things often, and change ("Change in all things is sweet"); and learning and wonder.

scenes.title: Benefits, Imitation and Self-Love
scenes.summary: Conferring and receiving benefits are pleasant, and setting others right. Imitations, in painting, sculpture and poetry, please because we learn that this is that; so do reversals and narrow escapes. Like delights in like, as the proverbs say, and everyone loves himself, his works, his children, and the appearance of wisdom.

scenes.title: Rule, Rebuke and Laughter
scenes.summary: It is pleasant to rule, to rebuke, and to spend one's time where one is at one's best, as Euripides says; and play, relaxation and laughter are pleasant, and so are laughable people, words and deeds, discussed separately in the Poetics.
